text: A man once survived with an opening into his stomach.
But why didn't his stomach digest itself?
Mucus is only part of the answer.
Surface cells release bicarbonate into that mucus.
It neutralizes acid close to the stomach wall, helping keep the cell surface much less acidic than the contents above.
The mucus also helps slow acid from reaching the cells.
Other defenses help too, including tightly joined cells and surface repair.
That patient's name was Alexis Saint Martin.
The experiments were real, but ethically troubling.
His story revealed digestion, not the modern explanation of this protective barrier.
